- If sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or add downward bias.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and prices drop sharply, model often underestimates the fall; increase downward adjustment or add volatility buffer.
- After a price spike (e.g., >78), model frequently overcorrects with a steep downward slope; cap forecast decline to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish, model often lags in adjusting downward; apply early correction if sentiment drops below 0.33.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., from 80 to 70+), model tends to overpredict continuation; reduce forecast momentum after 3–5 days of high prices.
- For 30-day forecasts, if history shows volatility clustering (e.g., 3+ consecutive drops), model often underestimates volatility; add 5–10% buffer to forecast range.
- If sentiment is neutral (0.33–0.67) and price is trending, model often fails to capture momentum; adjust forecast to align with sentiment direction, not just history.
